summary.text: Take \(n=14\). The condition that \(2k+1\) be prime restricts \(1\le k<14\) to \(k=1,2,3,5,6,8,9,11\), for which the prime-count pairs in \(((k-1)14,14k]\) and \((14k,14(k+1)]\) are respectively \((6,3),(3,4),(4,3),(3,4),(4,2),(4,1),(1,4),(2,3)\); none are equal, so the required witness does not exist despite \(14>1\) and \(14\ne8\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(\pi(x)\) denote the number of primes at most \(x\). We disprove the strengthened existence assertion in the conjecture by taking
\[
n=14.
\]
Certainly \(14>1\) and \(14\ne 8\), so if the conjecture were true, there would have to be an integer \(k\) such that
\[
0<k<14,\qquad 2k+1\text{ is prime},
\]
and
\[
\pi(14k)-\pi(14(k-1))
=
\pi(14(k+1))-\pi(14k).
\tag{1}
\]
The two sides of (1) count the primes in the adjacent intervals
\[
(14(k-1),14k]\quad\text{and}\quad(14k,14(k+1)],
\]
respectively.

We now compute the numbers of primes in the consecutive intervals of length \(14\) that can occur. For \(j=0,1,\ldots,13\), put
\[
B_j=(14j,14(j+1)]
\]
and let \(b_j\) be the number of primes in \(B_j\). The primes in these intervals are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
j & B_j & \text{primes in }B_j \\ \hline
0 &(0,14]     &2,3,5,7,11,13\\
1 &(14,28]    &17,19,23\\
2 &(28,42]    &29,31,37,41\\
3 &(42,56]    &43,47,53\\
4 &(56,70]    &59,61,67\\
5 &(70,84]    &71,73,79,83\\
6 &(84,98]    &89,97\\
7 &(98,112]   &101,103,107,109\\
8 &(112,126]  &113\\
9 &(126,140]  &127,131,137,139\\
10&(140,154]  &149,151\\
11&(154,168]  &157,163,167\\
12&(168,182]  &173,179,181\\
13&(182,196]  &191,193
\end{array}
\]
This table is obtained by the elementary finite primality test: a number at most \(196\) is prime exactly when it is at least \(2\) and has no prime divisor at most its square root. Since \(\sqrt{196}=14\), it is enough throughout the table to test divisibility by \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), omitting a prospective divisor when its square already exceeds the number being tested. These divisibility tests show both that every displayed number is prime and that every undisplayed integer in the indicated ranges is composite. Thus the corresponding sequence of interval counts is
\[
(b_0,b_1,\ldots,b_{13})
=(6,3,4,3,3,4,2,4,1,4,2,3,3,2).
\tag{2}
\]
Equivalently, the relevant values of the prime-counting function at multiples of \(14\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrrrrrrrr}
x&0&14&28&42&56&70&84&98&112&126&140&154&168&182&196\\ \hline
\pi(x)&0&6&9&13&16&19&23&25&29&30&34&36&39&42&44.
\end{array}
\]
Taking consecutive differences in this second table gives exactly (2).

Because \(0<k<14\), there are only the thirteen possibilities \(k=1,2,\ldots,13\). For a given such \(k\), the left side of (1) is \(b_{k-1}\), while the right side is \(b_k\). The complete comparison is
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
k&b_{k-1}&b_k&\text{equal?}\\ \hline
1&6&3&\text{no}\\
2&3&4&\text{no}\\
3&4&3&\text{no}\\
4&3&3&\text{yes}\\
5&3&4&\text{no}\\
6&4&2&\text{no}\\
7&2&4&\text{no}\\
8&4&1&\text{no}\\
9&1&4&\text{no}\\
10&4&2&\text{no}\\
11&2&3&\text{no}\\
12&3&3&\text{yes}\\
13&3&2&\text{no}.
\end{array}
\]
Consequently, among all integers satisfying \(0<k<14\), equation (1) can hold only for
\[
k=4\quad\text{or}\quad k=12.
\]
Neither value satisfies the additional primality condition. Indeed,
\[
2\cdot4+1=9=3^2
\]
and
\[
2\cdot12+1=25=5^2,
\]
so both numbers are composite.

It follows that for \(n=14\) there is no integer \(k\) with \(0<k<n\) for which \(2k+1\) is prime and the two adjacent length-\(n\) intervals have equal prime counts. Since \(14>1\) and \(14\ne8\), this directly contradicts the conjecture's “moreover” assertion. The full conjecture is a conjunction containing that assertion for every \(n\), so failure at \(n=14\) disproves it, regardless of whether the separate positivity assertion \(a(14)>0\) holds.
